annotations.keyFindings: Relatives called at six weeks accepted support more often than relatives called at two weeks (34 percent against 21 percent); relatives called early often asked to be called later.
annotations.limitations: Two hospices of different size and staffing, so timing is confounded by site; no grief outcomes.

annotations.keyFindings: Replacing a written invitation with a proactive volunteer call was followed by a rise in uptake from 18 percent to 37 percent, while the comparison service stayed at 16 percent.
annotations.limitations: Controlled before-after design; the two services served different populations; family experience of the call was not measured.

annotations.keyFindings: With a brief risk screen at the time of death, 19 percent of relatives were rated high risk; uptake was 52 percent among high-risk relatives offered a social worker call and 13 percent among others sent a letter.
annotations.limitations: Risk level and outreach method changed together, so their effects cannot be separated; screening was completed for 71 percent of deaths; prediction of prolonged grief not assessed.

annotations.keyFindings: Uptake was 22 percent overall, 14 percent among men against 27 percent among women, 9 percent among relatives who needed an interpreter and 12 percent among relatives living more than 50 kilometres away.
annotations.limitations: One hospice; service records only; support obtained elsewhere was not captured.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 14 studies, mostly before-after designs, proactive personal contact was the strategy most consistently followed by higher uptake; evidence on timing was mixed and no study tested text messages or interpreter-supported outreach.
annotations.limitations: Search ended in March 2022; most included studies at serious risk of bias; outcome definitions varied and prevented pooling.

annotations.keyFindings: A text message invitation with a follow-up call gave 41 percent replies and 29 percent uptake, against 22 percent uptake after letters the previous year; relatives over 75 more often took up support only after the call.
annotations.limitations: Historical comparison in one service; relatives without a mobile number on record were not invited by text.

annotations.keyFindings: Relatives who declined most often felt supported by family and friends, were not ready when the offer came, did not know what support involved, or faced travel and working-hours barriers; several men would have accepted one-to-one support rather than a group.
annotations.limitations: Forms returned by a minority of those who declined, so the reasons may not represent the whole group.

claims.text: In a controlled before-after comparison, replacing a written invitation with a proactive telephone call was followed by a rise in uptake of bereavement support from 18 percent to 37 percent, while uptake in the comparison service stayed at 16 percent.
claims.passage: uptake of any bereavement support rose from 18 percent to 37 percent in the intervention service and was unchanged at 16 percent in the comparison service
claims.interpretation: Proactive personal contact has the clearest signal; the design is not randomised, so the size of the change is a planning value only.

claims.text: In a comparison between two hospices, relatives called at six weeks after the death accepted support more often than relatives called at two weeks (34 percent against 21 percent).
claims.passage: Of 388 relatives called at two weeks, 21 percent accepted support, compared with 34 percent of 402 relatives called at six weeks.
claims.interpretation: Earlier calls may not raise uptake; the comparison is confounded by site.

claims.text: A systematic review of 14 studies searched to March 2022 found proactive personal contact to be the strategy most consistently followed by higher uptake, with mixed evidence on timing and no study of text messages or interpreter-supported outreach.
claims.passage: Proactive personal contact was the strategy most consistently followed by higher uptake. Evidence on timing was mixed, and no included study tested text messages or interpreter-supported outreach.
claims.interpretation: An update from March 2022 onward can add newer studies of text messages and targeted outreach.

claims.text: At one hospice, uptake of bereavement support was 14 percent among men against 27 percent among women, and 9 percent among relatives who needed an interpreter.

claims.interpretation: The review should extract uptake by sex, language and distance wherever it is reported.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Proactive personal contact was followed by higher uptake of bereavement support in a controlled before-after comparison (18 to 37 percent) and was the most consistent signal in a systematic review of 14 studies searched to March 2022. Evidence on timing is mixed: one two-hospice comparison favoured a first call at six weeks over two weeks, but site differences confound it. Risk screening concentrated uptake among relatives rated high risk, and a text message invitation with a follow-up call was followed by higher uptake than letters in one service. Men, relatives who need an interpreter and relatives living far away take up support less often. No record measured grief outcomes. The evidence supports a rapid review that updates the 2023 review from March 2022 and extracts results by sex, language and distance.
gradeRationale: Non-randomised comparisons from single services, a systematic review whose included studies were mostly at serious risk of bias, and descriptive service records; the direction for proactive contact is consistent, but risk of bias is serious and uptake definitions differ.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.
